# Simultaneous cap BM equality: nested cones and a simplex rigidity theorem
It does not assert that an OC extremizer satisfies its equality premises.
All volumes in this note are ordinary d-dimensional Lebesgue volumes.

## 1. Two nested homothetic truncations force an actual cone

Let D be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, let u!=0, and
write m=min_D u.x and h=max_D u.x. Suppose

    m<=a<b<h,
    D_a=D intersect {u.x>=a},
    D_b=D intersect {u.x>=b},
    D_b=lambda D_a+v                                      (1)

for a positive homothety. Both truncations have positive volume. Their
volumes are strictly different: D has an open set in the band a<u.x<b,
so 0<lambda<1. Then there is a UNIQUE exposed support point p of D in
direction u and

    lambda=(h-b)/(h-a),
    v=(1-lambda)p,
    D_a=conv(p, D intersect {u.x=a}).                     (2)

Here is a complete proof, including the self-similarity step. The common
top support face F=D intersect {u.x=h} satisfies F=lambda F+v by(1).
Taking diameters gives diam F=lambda diam F, so F is the singleton {p}.
Equation(1) on this face gives v=(1-lambda)p. Translate p to0, and use
height t=h-u.x, which is a nonnegative linear coordinate after that
translation. Put A=h-a>0 and B=h-b in (0,A), and L=D_a-p. Then

    L intersect {t<=B}=lambda L.

The maximum t on these two sides is B and lambda A respectively, so
B=lambda A. For t in (0,A], denote by S(t) the transverse section of L
at height t, expressed in a fixed linear splitting of R^d into its
height coordinate and ker u. The exact homothety identity gives

    S(lambda t)=lambda S(t).                            (3)

Since0 belongs to L and L is convex, for 0<s<t<=A,

    S(s) contains (s/t)S(t).

Consequently the normalized sections S(t)/t decrease by inclusion as
t increases, while(3) says their values at lambda t and t are identical.
They are therefore constant throughout [lambda t,t]. Applying this to
t=A,lambda A,lambda^2 A,... proves

    S(t)=(t/A)S(A) for every 0<t<=A.

The only section at height0 is {0}, by the uniqueness of the top face.
Thus L is exactly the cone from0 over S(A), proving(2). This argument
also covers a=m; if equality is possible there, the resulting base
section is necessarily (d-1)-dimensional because D_a is full dimensional.

Conversely, if D_a is the cone in(2), every higher nonempty truncation
D_b, a<b<h, is the corresponding positive homothetic copy of D_a.
No smoothness, polytopality, or rationality has been assumed.

## 2. Exact one-direction classification on a homothetic family

Let d>=2. Suppose A_j=a_j D+v_j for j=1,...,N, where |D|=1,
a_j>0, theta_j>0, sum theta_j=1, and put

    s=sum theta_j a_j,
    v_0=sum theta_j v_j,
    K=sum theta_j A_j=sD+v_0.

Fix one closed halfspace H={u.x>=b}, u!=0. Its normalized endpoint
thresholds in D are

    q_j=(b-u.v_j)/a_j,
    q_0=(b-u.v_0)/s=sum_j (theta_j a_j/s) q_j.             (4)

Assume every endpoint cut is PROPER: m<q_j<h, where m=min_D u.x and
h=max_D u.x. Thus both sides of each endpoint cut have positive volume.
The source cut is also proper. Then exact equality in the captured-side
BM comparison

    |K intersect H|^(1/d)
       =sum_j theta_j |A_j intersect H|^(1/d)             (5)

holds if and only if one of the following alternatives holds:

(a) All q_j are equal.

(b) They are not all equal, and D intersect {u.x>=q_min}, q_min=min_j q_j,
    is a cone with its unique apex at the support point of D in direction u.

Proof of necessity: the Minkowski sum of the endpoint cap sections is
contained in K intersect H. Equality(5) forces equality in the ordinary
positive-volume Brunn--Minkowski inequality for those cap sections.
The standard equality case of that classical theorem says that these
full-dimensional cap bodies are pairwise positive homothetic copies.
For a finite sum this follows from the two-body equality case: a strict
inequality for any selected pair would remain strict after adding the
other positive-weight bodies. Since A_j intersect H is a positive
homothetic translate of D intersect {u.x>=q_j}, the normalized cap
truncations are pairwise homothetic. If q_min<q_max, Section1 applied
to these two truncations proves alternative(b).

For sufficiency in(a), the normalized cap is the same set at every
endpoint, and both Minkowski inclusion and BM are equalities. For(b),
write P for the cone apex and L=D intersect {u.x>=q_min}. For any
q in [q_min,q_max], cone geometry gives

    D intersect {u.x>=q}
       =P+rho(q)(L-P),
    rho(q)=(h-q)/(h-q_min).

The function rho is affine. Equation(4) gives
s rho(q_0)=sum theta_j a_j rho(q_j), which proves equality of the actual
source cap with the Minkowski sum of the endpoint caps. Their volume
roots consequently add exactly, proving(5).

The ordinary positive-volume BM equality characterization is the only
standard equality theorem invoked in this section; the nested-cap
rigidity it produces is proved in Section1. The scalar cap fractions
|D intersect {u.x>=q_j}| are unequal exactly when the q_j are unequal,
because the cap volume is strictly decreasing on (m,h).

## 3. A finite cone cover about an interior point forces a simplex

Let D be a full-dimensional convex body in R^d with0 in int D. Suppose
there are nonzero normals u_1,...,u_m and strictly positive numbers
beta_1,...,beta_m satisfying

    sum_i beta_i u_i=0.                                  (6)

For each i suppose there is epsilon_i>0 such that

    D intersect {u_i.x>=-epsilon_i}
       =conv(p_i, D intersect {u_i.x=-epsilon_i}),        (7)

where u_i.p_i>-epsilon_i. Then D is a d-simplex. Its vertices are exactly
the DISTINCT points among p_1,...,p_m. Repeated labels are allowed. In
addition, the normals span all of R^d. Thus these hypotheses cannot
hold for a positive circuit whose normal span has rank less than d.

First, (7) shows that p_i is the unique maximum of u_i on that cap.
Outside the cap u_i.x<-epsilon_i, so p_i is also the UNIQUE exposed
maximum of u_i on all D. In particular, it is an extreme point of D.
Because0 is interior, max_D u_i.x>0, so u_i.p_i>0.

Every extreme point x of D equals at least one p_i. Indeed(6) implies
u_i.x>=0 for at least one i; otherwise the positive weighted sum of
these real numbers would be negative. This puts x strictly above the
base plane of the cone(7). If x!=p_i, the cone representation places x
on a nontrivial segment from p_i to a point of its base, with both
endpoints in D and x strictly between them. That contradicts extremality.
Thus D has only the finitely many exposed extreme points in the list p_i.

For completeness, this proves D=conv{p_i} without assuming a polytope
in advance. Otherwise separate a point of D outside this finite convex
hull by a linear functional l, so max_D l>max_i l(p_i). The compact
maximal face of D for l has an extreme point of D: successively maximize
a basis of coordinate functionals within that face; the final common
maximal face is a singleton, and extremality passes from a face to D.
This produces an extreme point with l-value greater than every l(p_i),
contradicting the preceding paragraph.

Write the distinct vertices as P={p^(1),...,p^(k)}. For each p^(j), choose
one label i with p_i=p^(j). Every other vertex satisfies

    u_i.p^(ell)<=-epsilon_i<0,          ell!=j,           (8)

since a different extreme point strictly above the base plane would
lie on the nontrivial cone segment just excluded. Hence0 does not
belong to conv(P minus {p^(j)}). Every convex representation of0 by
vertices must use EVERY vertex. Yet Caratheodory's elementary reduction
gives a representation using at most d+1: if a representation uses
more, an affine dependence of its points permits varying the weights
while preserving their sum and barycenter until at least one positive
weight becomes zero, and repetition finishes the reduction. It follows
that k<=d+1. Full dimension gives k>=d+1, so k=d+1 and D is a simplex.

Finally let U=span{u_i}, of dimension r. Project the vertices orthogonally
to U. Their projections are distinct, because(8) and u_i.p_i>0 distinguish
each vertex from all others. The origin belongs to their convex hull,
and(8) implies again that every representation of0 by these projected
points needs every one of the d+1 points. Caratheodory in U gives d+1<=r+1.
Since r<=d, necessarily r=d. This proves the rank assertion.

## 4. Simultaneous captured-side BM equality implies simplex rigidity

Let d>=2, A_1,...,A_N be full-dimensional convex bodies in R^d,
theta_j>0 with sum theta_j=1, and let K contain sum theta_j A_j. Assume
whole-body BM is exactly tight:

    |K|^(1/d)=sum_j theta_j |A_j|^(1/d).                  (9)

Let y belong to int K. Let H_i={x:u_i.(x-y)>=0}, where the nonzero u_i
have a strictly positive balance(6). Suppose for EVERY i:

* every endpoint cut A_j intersect H_i is proper;
* the normalized endpoint fractions
  |A_j intersect H_i|/|A_j| are NOT all equal as j varies;
* the actual source captured-side comparison is an equality:

    |K intersect H_i|^(1/d)
       =sum_j theta_j |A_j intersect H_i|^(1/d).         (10)

Then K and every A_j are homothetic d-simplices, and span{u_i}=R^d.

Here are the normalization and all averaging identities explicitly.
Set a_j=|A_j|^(1/d) and s=sum theta_j a_j. Ordinary BM and(9) force
K=sum theta_j A_j, since a strict inclusion between full-dimensional
compact convex bodies has strictly different volume. The positive-volume
BM equality case makes all A_j homothetic. Define

    D=(K-y)/s.

Then |D|=1 and0 in int D, and there are vectors v_j with

    A_j=a_j D+v_j,
    sum_j theta_j v_j=y.                                (11)

For direction i, the normalized threshold in endpoint j is

    q_ij=[u_i.y-u_i.v_j]/a_j.

Its weighted mean is EXACTLY the source through-point threshold0:

    sum_j (theta_j a_j/s) q_ij
      =[u_i.y-u_i.sum_j theta_j v_j]/s=0.                (12)

The unequal-fraction hypothesis and strict monotonicity of cap volume
imply that the q_ij are not all equal. Thus(12) gives
q_i,min<0<q_i,max. By(10) and Section2, the larger cap
D intersect {u_i.x>=q_i,min} is a cone at its unique exposed apex p_i.
Put epsilon_i=-q_i,min>0. All hypotheses of Section3 now hold, including
a larger cone cap in EVERY balancing direction. Hence D is a simplex
and the normal span is full. Equations(11) yield the stated conclusion.

This proof uses the given actual halfspaces throughout; no continuous
centroid is rounded and no sampled lattice sum is replaced by an integral.
It is local rigidity under exact equalities, not a variational theorem
forcing an arbitrary mixed-integer body to satisfy(9)--(10).

## 5. Sharpness and necessary limits of the hypotheses

The simplex conclusion is attained. Let T be any d-simplex, g its
centroid, D=T-g, and let l_0,...,l_d be the linear parts of its barycentric
coordinate functions. Then sum_i l_i=0. The through-origin halfspaces
H_i={l_i(x)>=0} form a positive circuit and each cuts the canonical
centroid cap. Choose a sufficiently small vector v such that
l_i(v)!=0 for every i; a finite union of proper hyperplanes cannot cover
a neighborhood, so such vectors exist. Put A=D+v, B=D-v with weights1/2,
so K=D. All endpoint cuts are proper for small v. For each i the two
normalized thresholds are -l_i(v) and l_i(v), and the larger truncation
is still a cone at vertex i: in barycentric coordinates its threshold
remains strictly between0 and1. Section2 proves exact captured-side BM
equality for all d+1 caps simultaneously, with unequal fractions in
every direction. Thus the rigidity statement is not vacuous.

Positive balance supplies the through-point cover used here; independent
normals alone do not supply it.
For an exact planar example take

    A=[0,1]^2,
    B=A+(1/10,0),
    K=(A+B)/2=A+(1/20,0),
    H_1={x+y>=3/2}, H_2={x-y>=1/2}.

The two cap boundaries meet at y_0=(1,1/2), which lies in int K. Their
normals (1,1),(1,-1) are independent but have no positive balance.
For BOTH directions the cap areas on A,B,K are respectively

    1/8, 9/50, 121/800.

Their square roots satisfy
sqrt(121/800)=(sqrt(1/8)+sqrt(9/50))/2 exactly. The endpoint fractions
are unequal, cuts are proper, and whole-body BM is tight. Nevertheless
K is a square, not a simplex. These are two separate conical vertex
caps of a square; their halfspaces do not cover it.

The requirement that EVERY balancing direction have unequal endpoint
fractions also matters. Concentric homothetic copies of an arbitrary
body have equal normalized endpoint fractions in every through-center
direction and attain all corresponding side-BM equalities. Such a body
need not be a simplex. The theorem does not eliminate these constant
fraction directions by assuming them away in a general OC argument.

There is also a nonconcentric counterexample if even one balancing
direction is allowed to have equal endpoint fractions. In dimension two
let

    D=conv{(1,0),(-1,1),(-2,0),(-1,-1)},
    v=(0,1/10), A=D+v, B=D-v, K=D,
    u_1=(1,1/4), u_2=(1,-1/4), u_3=(-1,0),
    H_i={u_i.x>=0}.

The origin is interior, all endpoint cuts are proper, and
u_1+u_2+2u_3=0 is a full-rank positive circuit. For directions1,2, the
normalized endpoint thresholds are plus/minus1/40, so their fractions
are unequal. The common exposed apex is (1,0); all other vertices have
u_i-value at most -3/4. Therefore each outer cap at threshold -1/40 is
an actual cone at that apex, and Section2 gives side-BM equality in both
directions. For direction3, u_3.v=0, so its normalized thresholds and
fractions are equal and its side-BM equality also holds. Whole-body BM
is tight. Yet D has four vertices. This shows why a varying subset of
the directions cannot simply replace the full balancing family.

For reference, |D|=3, the source areas in directions1,2 equal32/63, and
their endpoint areas equal (32/63)(1 plus/minus1/40)^2. The source and
both endpoint areas in direction3 equal5/2. These are optional exact
checks; the cone argument establishes the equality geometrically.

## 6. A partial-family apex bound that does not assume positive balance

Let D be full dimensional with0 in its interior. Suppose it has finitely
many cone caps of the form(7), each extending strictly beyond0, but do
not assume(6). Let k be the number of DISTINCT apex points among them.
Then k<=d+1. If k=d+1, D is a simplex with precisely those vertices.
This also applies to the varying directions of Section4 if other
directions happen to have equal endpoint fractions.

As in Section3, each apex is an exposed extreme point and, for its own
normal, every other extreme point has value at most -epsilon<0. Every
representation of0 as a convex combination of extreme points must
therefore include that apex. A compact finite-dimensional convex body
is the convex hull of its extreme points: an elementary induction on
dimension proves this by writing an interior point as a combination of
two boundary points, then applying the induction in proper supporting
faces; extreme points of a face are extreme in the whole body. Thus0
has a finite such representation. Caratheodory reduces it to at most
d+1 extreme points, while every cone apex must remain present. This
proves k<=d+1.

If k=d+1, this reduced representation uses exactly the apex set
P={p_1,...,p_(d+1)} with positive weights alpha_j and sum alpha_j p_j=0.
These points are affinely independent: otherwise an affine dependence
would reduce the positive representation further, omitting an apex,
which is impossible. Thus every x in R^d has affine coordinates
x=sum_j t_j p_j with sum t_j=1. Choose an index i maximizing t_i/alpha_i,
and choose a cone-cap normal u_i exposing p_i. Since u_i.p_j<0 for j!=i,

    u_i.x
      =sum_(j!=i) alpha_j (t_j/alpha_j-t_i/alpha_i) u_i.p_j
      >=0.

The identity uses sum alpha_j u_i.p_j=0. Hence the through-origin
halfspaces of these d+1 cone caps cover all of R^d, even though positive
balance was not assumed. Any extreme point of D must consequently
lie strictly inside at least one cone cap relative to its base plane,
and must be that cap's apex by the segment argument of Section3. There
are no additional extreme points; D=conv P is the claimed simplex.

The nonconcentric quadrilateral above has only ONE distinct varying
apex, despite two independent varying normals. It is consistent with
this partial-family bound and illustrates why labels or normal rank
must not be substituted for the number of distinct indispensable apices.
